title: Is Tithing Required for Christians Today?
paragraphs: Is Tithing Required for Christians Today?
There are believers quietly carrying guilt every single Sunday.
Not because they cheated someone.
Not because they denied Jesus.
Not because they stopped praying.
But because they looked at their bank account… and felt like they failed God.
Ten percent.
That number has haunted Christians for generations.
Some were taught that if they did not tithe exactly ten percent, heaven itself would tighten against them.
Others were told financial struggle was proof they were “robbing God.”
Some gave faithfully for years while secretly drowning in debt.
Others stopped giving entirely because manipulation exhausted their spirit.
And somewhere in the middle of all the noise… sincere believers are asking a painfully honest question:
Is tithing actually required for Christians today?
Not emotionally.
Not traditionally.
Biblically.
What does Scripture truly say?
Not church culture.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
The Word of God.
Because if God commanded it, we should obey it.
And if people distorted it, we need courage to admit it.
This conversation matters more than money.
It reveals how we see God Himself.
A demanding collector?
Or a loving Father forming generous hearts?
The tension becomes even heavier when people discover something shocking:
Most Christians have never actually studied what the biblical tithe truly was.
Not historically.
Not contextually.
Not covenantally.
And when you finally slow down enough to examine Scripture carefully… the picture becomes far deeper than most people realize.
The first time “tithe” appears in Scripture is not under Moses.
It appears with Abraham.
Genesis 14 tells the story of Abram rescuing Lot after a regional war. After the victory, Abram encountered Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High.
Then Scripture says:
“and he gave him a tenth of everything.” — Genesis 14:20
The Hebrew word used is “מַעֲשֵׂר” (ma'aser), meaning “a tenth.”
But notice something critically important.
This was not a command.
This was not a recurring law.
This was not a temple obligation.
Abram voluntarily gave from war spoils after a military victory.
Nothing in the text says all believers for all generations were commanded to imitate this as binding law.
Then comes Jacob.
In Genesis 28:22, Jacob says:
“of all that You give me I will surely give a tenth to You.”
Again, voluntary.
Again, not commanded.
Again, before the Mosaic Law.
Then centuries later came Israel’s covenant at Sinai.
This is where everything changes.
The tithe became part of the Mosaic covenant given specifically to national Israel.
And this is where many modern conversations accidentally become historically inaccurate.
Because biblically speaking, the tithe was not merely about putting money into a religious offering basket.
The tithe in ancient Israel was deeply connected to:
land,
agriculture,
Levites,
temple service,
national festivals,
and caring for the poor.
Leviticus 27:30 says:
“Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD’S.”
Notice the wording.
Produce.
Seed.
Fruit.
Agricultural increase.
Why?
Because Israel was an agrarian covenant nation.
The tithe sustained the Levitical priesthood because the Levites did not receive tribal land inheritance like the other tribes.
Numbers 18:21 says:
“To the Levites I have given every tithe in Israel for an inheritance.”
The tithe was part of Israel’s covenant structure.
And historically, Israel actually practiced multiple tithes.
One supported Levites.
Another funded national worship festivals.
Another supported the vulnerable every third year.
When all calculations are examined together, many scholars estimate Israel’s giving obligations often exceeded twenty percent annually, not merely ten.
That surprises many people.
Because much of modern teaching oversimplifies the biblical system.
Then comes the verse almost everyone has heard.
Malachi 3.
“Will a man rob God? Yet you are robbing Me.”
The fear in that verse has controlled countless believers.
Some pastors thunder it.
Some churches weaponize it.
Some Christians panic whenever finances become difficult because they assume God is cursing them.
But context matters.
Malachi was speaking to covenant Israel under the Mosaic Law.
The priests had become corrupt.
The nation neglected covenant responsibilities.
The temple system was suffering.
This was not originally addressed to New Covenant Gentile believers living after Christ’s resurrection.
That does not make the passage irrelevant.
But it absolutely affects how we interpret it.
Because Christians are not under the Mosaic covenant as their governing covenant before God.
That statement alone unsettles some people.
But Scripture repeatedly teaches it.
Romans 6:14:
“For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under law but under grace.”
Galatians 3 explains the Law served a temporary covenant purpose leading toward Christ.
Hebrews explains the priesthood changed.
The covenant changed.
The sacrificial system changed.
Everything changed through Jesus.
Hebrews 7 becomes extremely important here because it discusses Melchizedek, Abraham, priesthood, and tithes.
Some use Hebrews 7 to argue Christians must tithe because Abraham tithed before the Law.
But Hebrews 7 is not commanding Christians to practice mandatory ten-percent giving.
The chapter’s actual focus is proving Christ’s superior priesthood through the order of Melchizedek.
The point is theological superiority.
Not establishing New Covenant tithing legislation.
Then comes the question many avoid asking directly:
Did Jesus command Christians to tithe?
Jesus mentioned tithing in passages like Matthew 23:23.
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law.”
But remember:
Jesus was speaking to Jews still living under the Mosaic covenant before the cross.
The New Covenant had not yet been inaugurated through His death and resurrection.
And importantly, Jesus criticized legalistic tithing without justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
He exposed outward religious precision with inward spiritual emptiness.
Then we arrive at the New Testament church.
And something fascinating happens.
The apostles give extensive instruction about generosity.
But nowhere do they explicitly command Christians to follow a mandatory ten-percent tithe law.
Instead, the emphasis radically shifts toward willing, cheerful, sacrificial generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 becomes foundational.
The Greek text says:
“Ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ”
Transliterated:
“Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia.”
Translation:
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart.”
Then Paul continues:
“not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.”
The Greek phrase “μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης” (mē ex anankēs) literally means “not from compulsion” or “not under coercion.”
That matters deeply.
Because manipulation can produce offerings… while still damaging hearts.
God is not merely after transactions.
He desires transformed people.
Under the New Covenant, generosity becomes internal before it becomes numerical.
The New Testament vision is actually more challenging than legalistic percentage giving.
Because the question shifts from:
“What is the minimum percentage required?”
To:
“Does Jesus truly own everything I have?”
That changes everything.
Some believers can faithfully give ten percent joyfully.
Others may temporarily be unable because of crushing hardship.
Others may be called to radical generosity far beyond ten percent.
In Acts, some believers sold property to meet urgent needs.
The New Testament model is not stinginess.
It is not greed.
It is not selfish consumer Christianity.
But neither is it fear-driven religious taxation.
It is Spirit-led generosity flowing from love.
And honestly… this exposes something uncomfortable in many hearts.
Sometimes people ask whether tithing is required because they desperately want permission to give nothing.
Other times people defend mandatory tithing because they fear church systems collapsing without it.
Both extremes can miss the deeper issue.
God has always been after the heart.
Jesus watched wealthy people give large offerings while a poor widow quietly gave two small coins.
He was not impressed by amount alone.
He saw surrender.
He saw trust.
He saw love.
And this is where many wounded believers need healing.
Some of you were spiritually manipulated.
You were made to feel cursed whenever finances became difficult.
You were pressured publicly.
Shamed emotionally.
Measured financially.
Some of you gave from fear instead of worship.
Others now struggle to trust any conversation about giving at all.
But abuse does not erase biblical generosity.
And correction does not mean rebellion.
The answer is not greed.
The answer is truth.
The early church absolutely supported ministry.
Paul taught that workers deserve support.
Believers shared resources.
Christians cared for widows, missionaries, struggling saints, and local assemblies.
Biblical generosity is real Christianity.
But the New Testament consistently emphasizes willingness rather than compulsion.
Love rather than fear.
Joy rather than manipulation.
And maybe that terrifies some people because percentages feel safer than surrender.
A strict number can make us feel spiritually secure.
“Just tell me the amount.”
But Jesus keeps reaching deeper.
Because a person can tithe meticulously while still loving money more than God.
The Pharisees proved that.
And another believer may give imperfectly yet genuinely trust Christ with their life.
So… is tithing required for Christians today?
If by “required” we mean a binding Mosaic covenant law commanding every Christian to give exactly ten percent under threat of divine curse… the New Testament does not explicitly teach that.

But if the question is whether Christians should be radically generous, sacrificial, supportive of God’s work, compassionate toward the poor, and willing to steward finances for Christ’s kingdom… absolutely yes.
The issue is not whether God needs your money.
He owns everything already.
Psalm 24:1 says:
“The earth is the LORD’S, and all its fullness.”
The issue is whether money owns you.
Jesus said:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
That verse still cuts deep.
Because giving reveals trust.
Not perfectly.
But honestly.
Some people spend more monthly on entertainment than eternal things.
Some believers will finance every appetite except the Kingdom of God.
Others quietly give while struggling financially themselves because they genuinely love Jesus.
And heaven sees all of it.
This conversation was never truly about percentages.
It was always about worship.
About lordship.
About whether Jesus is Savior only… or also Master.
And maybe right now the Holy Spirit is exposing something deeper than your wallet.
Maybe He is revealing fear.
Control.
Distrust.
Greed.
Or perhaps wounds caused by spiritual abuse.
Do not harden your heart.
Bring all of it before Christ.
Because the Gospel changes even our relationship with possessions.
Jesus became poor so sinners could become spiritually rich.
The cross itself is the greatest act of giving the world has ever seen.
And when grace truly captures a human heart… generosity eventually follows.
Not because salvation is purchased.
But because transformed hearts stop clinging so tightly to temporary things.
Maybe this article challenged assumptions you carried for years.
Maybe it brought relief.
Maybe conviction.
Maybe discomfort.
Maybe freedom.
But do not run from Scripture.
Study it.
Search deeply.
Test everything carefully.
Because God is not afraid of honest questions.
And truth does not collapse under examination.
Someone reading your honesty may realize they are not alone.
One day, every dollar we protected will disappear… but every act of love done for Christ will echo into eternity.
